# Course workflow — issues, PRs, reviews, sprint deliverables

Course rules, not upstream Gitea ones. Source: the course site <https://csci-435-se.github.io/>
(Sprints pages) and `docs/sprint0/standards.md`. Everyone on the team, and every AI session, uses
the formats below so all issues and PRs look the same. The GitHub templates in `.github/` carry the
same formats; if they ever disagree with this page, fix the template.

AI disclosure has its own page: `AI-ASSISTANCE.md`.

## Current sprint: Sprint 1

- **Dates:** Sep 22 – Oct 8, 2026. Everything pushed and merged by **Oct 8, 11:59 PM**.
- **Points:** 100 (10% of the course grade).
- **Zero rule:** no merged PR (D4), no sprint report (D6) or no release (D7) means **0 for the
  whole sprint**.
- **Carries forward:** every Sprint 0 standard and convention still applies.

| # | Deliverable | Points | Who | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | Sprint backlog: a `Sprint 1` milestone with every selected issue on it | 10 | Team | GitHub milestone |
| D2 | Requirements spec for each issue (formats below), peer-reviewed by a teammate | 20 | Individual | Issue body |
| D3 | At least one non-trivial design decision per issue | 7 | Individual | Issue body |
| D4 | Code changes and PRs | 36 | Individual | PRs |
| D5 | AI logs | 7 | Individual | `ai-logs/sprint1/<github-username>/` |
| D6 | Sprint report | 10 | Team | `docs/sprint1/report.md` |
| D7 | Release: tag `v1.27.3-csci435-s1` plus a GitHub release | 2 | Team | Tags / Releases |
| D8 | Reflection survey | 8 | Individual | Blackboard/Zulip link |

- **D1 load:** each CSCI 435 student owns at least 2 medium issues; each CSCI 535 student owns at
  least 2 medium and 1 small. Every issue has exactly **one** assignee. Specs should be final by
  Sep 27.
- **D5:** conventions are in `ai-logs/README.md`. The folder must exist even if no AI was used. In
  that case, post an issue comment saying so. Log links go in **issue comments only**, never in PRs
  (`AI-ASSISTANCE.md`).
- **D7:** keep Sprint 0's base version (`v1.27.3-csci435-s0` → `v1.27.3-csci435-s1`), push the tag
  to origin, and write release notes listing the features, fixes and improvements.
- **Reviews:** each student reviews at least one PR per sprint. Over the semester, each student
  reviews every teammate at least once.
- **Extra credit:** up to 3 points per PR accepted by upstream Gitea.

## Branches and commits

- Branches: `feat/issue-<N>-short-description`, `fix/issue-<N>-short-description` or
  `chore/short-description` (`STUDENTS.md`). One issue per branch.
- Commit messages follow Conventional Commits and end with the issue number:
  `feat(repo): show empty state on releases page (#17)`. Add an
  `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer when AI helped; never `Co-Authored-By` or
  `Signed-off-by` (`AGENTS.md`). A human approves every commit before it is made.

### Before each implementation: sync with main

Every new branch starts from an up-to-date `main`. AI sessions run this before writing any code:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch -c feat/issue-<N>-short-description
```

To pick up new work on `main` for a branch that already exists, **merge, don't rebase**. Rebasing
or squashing after review has started is not allowed (`docs/sprint0/standards.md`):

```bash
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
```

Do this before opening the PR and again if `main` moves while it is in review. Never merge another
feature branch into yours.

### After merge: clean up

A PR is merged with a merge commit once it is approved, every review comment is addressed and CI
passes. Then:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git branch -d feat/issue-<N>-short-description               # local branch
git push origin --delete feat/issue-<N>-short-description    # or GitHub's "Delete branch" button
git fetch --prune                                            # drop stale remote-tracking refs
```

Also check that the issue closed (via `Closes #N`), is on the sprint milestone, and has its AI
Assistance comment. Then run `specstory sync` and file the session's log (see `ai-logs/README.md`).

## Issue format: feature (user story)

Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user-story.yaml`. The user story must meet INVEST: Independent,
Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

```markdown
## User Story
As a <role>, I want <capability> so that <benefit>.

## User Scenario
<A short concrete walk-through: who, where in the UI, what they do, what they see.>

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given <state>, when <action>, then <observable result>.
- [ ] AC2: ...
- [ ] AC3: ...            (at least 3; each has a clear pass/fail result)

## Out of Scope
- <What this issue deliberately does not do.>

## Open Questions
- <Unresolved questions, or "None".>

## Design Decision
**Decision:** <what was chosen>
**Alternatives Considered:** <at least one other option>
**Rationale:** <why this one>
**Consequences:** <trade-offs, follow-up work, what it makes harder>

## Scope
small | medium | large, and matching `scope:` label
```

## Issue format: bug report

Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug-report.yaml`.

```markdown
## Observed Behavior
## Expected Behavior
## Steps to Reproduce
1. ...
## Additional Information
<Version or commit, browser/OS, logs, screenshots.>
## Design Decision
<Same four fields as above: Decision, Alternatives Considered, Rationale, Consequences.>
```

- **Design Decision (D3):** fill it in once you've picked an approach, before opening the PR. Put
  a second decision under another `### Decision 2` heading. If a PR changes the decision, update
  the issue body.
- **Peer review (D2):** a teammate reads the spec and comments `Spec reviewed — <notes>` on the
  issue before implementation starts.

## Pull request format

Template: `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Title uses Conventional Commits, e.g.
`fix(issues): keep label filter after search`. Description sections:

1. `Closes #<N>`, which links the issue and closes it on merge.
2. **What changed:** the change in your own words.
3. **Why:** the problem, and which acceptance criteria (AC1…) it satisfies.
4. **How it was tested / Test strategy:** tests added or updated and why these ones. Name any
   change that can't be tested automatically and how it was checked by hand. Every behaviour change
   needs a new or updated test.
5. **CI / manual verification:** CI status, or the commands run and their results.
6. **Design:** one line pointing at the Design Decision in the issue, or a note on how it changed.
7. **AI assistance:** format in `AI-ASSISTANCE.md` §2, with **no log link**.

Per-PR grading (20 points): correctness against the acceptance criteria 6, test strategy with
explanation 5, description quality 4, CI or manual verification 3, review rubric posted 2.

## Code review rubric

The reviewer posts this as a **PR comment**, as well as the GitHub review itself. A copy-paste copy
is in `.github/code-review-rubric.md`, so keep the two in sync. Pull the branch and test it when you
can, say what you checked, and mark each point as required or optional
(`docs/community-governance.md`). Score each row against the issue's acceptance criteria. Anything
below 7 needs a note saying what would raise it.

```markdown
### Code Review — @reviewer-username

**Checked:** <what you ran or tried>

| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correctness — implements issue requirements | | |
| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | | |
| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | | |
| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | | |
| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | | |
| Overall — merge as-is? | | |
```

## Sprint report (D6) sections

`docs/sprint<N>/report.md`, following `docs/sprint0/report.md`:

- Team: names, GitHub usernames, project name, repository link.
- Sprint overview.
- Backlog: milestone link, plus a table of title, owner, points, scope and status.
- Requirements and design: when specs were done, what surprised you, design rationale.
- Completed issues: title, owner, PR link, author, reviewer, what changed.
- Test strategy, including untestable changes and why.
- AI tool usage per member: tools, session count, AI log folder link, and 2–3 sentences on lessons
  learned.
- Release: tag and release link.
- Risks and retrospective: what worked, what slowed the team down, Sprint 2 changes.
- Sprint 2 plan: initial ideas and carryover issues.

**Team Name:** GiCoffee

## Sprint Overview

Brief narrative: what the team set out to do and what was actually delivered. Be honest about scope changes

### What we planned to do

At the start of the sprint, we were hit with the problem that most issues were ambitious and large in scope, making it difficult to cleanly assign work between different members of the team.

A number of large issues, namely #7, #12, #23 and #25, were cut down into smaller medium and small issues that were easier to manage. The plan was to complete these large issues, with members who split the issues into smaller issues working on the backbone of the problem, and then distributing the issues among other members to complete them.

### Scope Changes

While we certainly got close to completing all of the aforementioned large issues, and managed to complete all 13 issues in the Sprint 1 milestone (#12 through its sub-issues #53, #54 and #55, plus #50, #51, #61, #62, #63, #64, #14, #34 and #35), larger than expected issues and requests from product owners made it difficult to achieve our goal. The request from the product owner to complete #14, or “Add a burndown chart to milestones with an ideal line and projected finish,” was one of the main reasons we had to change the scope of this sprint.

Issue #14 was a large issue, and with one of our team members completely devoted to this purpose, we had to change the scope of the sprint to ensure we are able to complete the main issues, and leave cleanup work for the next sprint. Because of this, #64 was only picked up on the last day of the sprint (PR #81), the keyboard shortcut issues (#56, #57) were deferred and moved out of the milestone, and #52 was moved to Sprint 2.

Fortunately, however, we were able to complete #12 and #14 in full, along with the core of #7 and #25 (#50, #51 and #61–#64), so we still consider this sprint to be a success. The remaining sub-issues (#52, #65 and #56–#60) carry over into Sprint 2.

## Requirements & Design

Were specs complete before coding started? Any surprises? Key design decisions and brief rationale

### State of issues at the start of the sprint

Most of the issues carried over from Sprint 0 (#7, #12, #14, #23, #25, #34, #35) were written as summaries or proposals, not in the Sprint 1 spec format. Each owner rewrote their issue into a User Story, User Scenario, numbered Acceptance Criteria, Out of Scope and Open Questions, and a teammate posted a "Spec Reviewed" comment on the issue before implementation started.

Surprises:

- #35 was sent back ("Spec Reviewed: Not yet") for numbered acceptance criteria and was approved after it was revised.
- #14's spec was refined late, after implementation had already started.
- The review of #64 found that one of its acceptance criteria was already met by #62.
- Close reasons (#12) needed a database change and reached into automatic closes (commits, cross-references and the API), which became its own sub-issue (#55).

### Key decisions that led to the splitting of Issues

- **#7 Overhauled notifications system** → #50 (filter), #51 (bulk actions), #52 (sort). #52 was moved to Sprint 2 because it needs a database migration and a queue change.
- **#12 Close reasons** → #53 (storage and backend), #54 (UI), #55 (automatic and API closes). The issue was split by layer so that the backend could be merged first and the UI could build on it.
- **#25 Make dropdowns Accessible** → #61 (menu web component), #62 (menu migration), #63 (multi-select ARIA), #64 (icon-only triggers), #65 (Playwright regression suite). #61 had to be merged before #62 could use it.
- **#23 Keyboard navigation/shortcuts** → #56–#60, all deferred to keep the sprint scope achievable.
- **#14, #34 and #35** were kept as single issues. #14 is large and counts as two medium issues.

### Key design decisions

- **#50:** "Mark all as read" respects the active filter.
- **#51:** "Select all" only selects the notifications in the current view, with an explicit "Select all N notifications in this view" link. Bulk actions never reach outside the active view.
- **#53:** `CloseIssue` becomes a wrapper over a new `CloseIssueWithReason`, so existing callers keep working unchanged.
- **#54:** Picking "Duplicate" or "Other" opens a small popup under the close button, and each close reason gets its own icon.
- **#55:** Automatic closes record a default reason (completed for issues, not planned for pull requests).
- **#61:** The menu is built as a custom element under `web_src/js/webcomponents/`, without Fomantic.
- **#62:** Only static, server-rendered, single-select menus are migrated.
- **#63:** The existing Fomantic dropdown patch is extended rather than replaced.
- **#34:** `?due=` is parsed once into deadline bounds that both the database search and the issue indexer use.
- **#35:** A member or outside collaborator without two-factor authentication is treated as a non-member of the organization until they enrol. This is a reversible lockout: nothing is deleted.
- **#14:** Each milestone's history is rebuilt when the chart is requested, by replaying its items' timeline comments (milestone changes, closes, merges and reopens), and served from a separate JSON endpoint that the page loads after it renders, instead of a daily snapshot table that would have no history for existing milestones.

## Test Strategy

What kinds of tests were written? Were there changes you couldn't test automatically? Why?

Tests were written against the acceptance criteria, often one test per criterion:

- **Go unit tests** for models and services, run against the test database: #67, #68, #69, #70, #72, #73, #76, #77
- **Integration tests** that go through the full HTTP request path: #67, #68, #69, #70, #72, #73, #76, #77
- **Vitest** frontend unit tests: #68, #70, #71, #72, #75, #77, #81
- **Playwright end-to-end tests**: #68, #70, #71, #74, #75, #77, #81 (#71 also added a WebKit/Safari run)

In #67 and #68, the tests themselves were checked by deliberately breaking key lines of code and confirming that a test failed.

Changes we couldn't test automatically: screen reader behavior can't be driven in CI, so the accessibility work (#62/#74, #63/#75, #64/#81) asserts the ARIA attributes and live-region text instead. #81 also adds a development-mode warning for any dropdown trigger without an accessible name; the reviewer ran it on a local build, page by page, to find triggers the tests don't cover. Visual layout was checked by hand and with screenshots (#68, #74), and the Firefox end-to-end run only happens in CI.

## Risks and Retrospective

What worked:

- Splitting the large issues into sub-issues gave each member at least two medium issues and let work happen in parallel.
- The "Spec Reviewed" step caught gaps before coding started (#35 was revised before it was approved).
- Writing tests per acceptance criterion, and checking the tests by deliberately breaking code (#67, #68), produced well-specified PRs.
- CodeRabbit, added mid-sprint, gave quick first-pass reviews on #71–#77, alongside the required human rubric reviews.

What slowed the team:

- Review bottleneck: most PRs were opened in the last three days of the sprint (#71–#81, Oct 6–8), and one required approval with only a few active reviewers slowed merging. Four PRs (#73, #76, #77, #81) were merged in the final hours, and #81 was opened on the last evening.
- #77's burndown test passes on SQLite, MySQL and MSSQL but fails on PostgreSQL in CI, because events in the same second come back in a different order. It was merged on the last day with that check still failing, and the fix carries over into Sprint 2.
- #14 was a large issue that took one member the whole sprint, and its spec was refined late.
- Open PRs fell 25 commits behind `main` as other PRs merged and had to be updated.
- AI logs committed inside feature PRs made the diffs 8,000–36,000 added lines long, which made them harder to review.
- CodeRabbit's autofix pushed a commit directly to a teammate's branch (#76).
- Codebase size: Gitea has about 40 service packages, 85 module packages, and more than 300 migrations, so concept location still takes much longer than expected.

Changes for Sprint 2:

- Open PRs by the middle of the sprint and request a reviewer when opening them, aiming for a review within 24 hours.
- Don't start a branch until the spec is "Approved".
- Commit AI logs in a separate chore PR, as #78 did.
- Use CodeRabbit as a first pass only, with no autofix on someone else's branch without the author's OK.
- Update the branch from `main` before requesting a review.

## Sprint 2 Plan

Brief ideas on the features the team intends to tackle; any setup still needed

We plan to fix #77's failing PostgreSQL burndown test first, then address #52 (sort notifications by reason or type, spec already posted), #65 (Playwright keyboard regression suite for dropdowns) and the keyboard shortcut issues under #23 (#56–#60) first, along with two small follow-ups from the #81 review (the merge-style button in the pull request merge box and the repository topics editor still have no accessible name), split between 2-3 members between each. This will not be a strict split, though it should help complete issues faster, akin to pair programming under the extreme programming paradigm.

If we complete these issues quicker than the end of the sprint, we will attempt to implement more medium term issues to the extent possible.

Add a burndown chart to milestones with an ideal line and projected finish date
## Summary
A Gitea milestone page shows only a progress bar and the current open and closed counts. There's no way to see how work progressed over the milestone's life, whether the team is on track for the due date, or when scope was added mid-way.

This feature adds a **burndown chart** to the milestone page. It compares the open items left each day against an **ideal line**, marks scope changes, and projects a **finish date** from the current pace. It helps teams running sprints or releases (like our own course sprints) spot a slipping milestone early, and helps leads explain *why*, for example because issues were added partway through.

## User Story
As a team lead, I want a burndown chart for each milestone comparing actual progress against an ideal pace so that I can tell early whether we'll finish by the due date and see when scope changed.

## User Scenario
A team lead opens their sprint milestone at `/{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}` a week before its due date. Above the issue list is a chart titled "Burndown" with a one-line summary: "Projected to finish on Oct 21, 2 days after the due date".
- The remaining line sits above the dashed ideal line from day 3 onwards. A ▲ on day 3 shows that two items were added to the milestone that day.
- Hovering day 3 lists them, "Added to milestone: #9 Support SSO" and "#10 Audit log", and the same list appears under the chart with links.
- The lead ticks "Include pull requests" to count the sprint's pull requests too, and the page URL gains `include_pulls=1`. They paste that URL into the team chat, and teammates who open it see the same chart.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given a milestone with items, when its page loads, then a chart shows the open items left at the end of each day as the **actual** line, and a straight **ideal** line from the first day with work down to zero on the due date.
- [ ] AC2: Given items that were closed and reopened, or moved between milestones, when the chart is drawn, then each past day's counts reflect the timeline events (milestone changes, closes, merges, reopens), and the last day matches the milestone's progress bar.
- [ ] AC3: Given items added to or removed from the milestone after its first day of work, then the chart marks those days (▲ added, ▼ removed).
- [ ] AC4: Given at least two days of history since work began and a falling count, then a projected finish date is drawn and stated, compared with the due date. With too little history, no burn-down, all work done, or a closed milestone, the projection is hidden and the summary says why.
- [ ] AC5: Given a day on which items changed, when the user hovers that day, then the items that changed are listed (closed, reopened, added, removed). The same list appears under the chart with links, because a chart tooltip can't hold links.
- [ ] AC6: Given the "Include pull requests" checkbox, then it is off by default, ticking it counts pull requests too, and its state is kept in the page URL (`include_pulls=1`) without changing the issue list's own filters.
- [ ] AC7: The edge cases behave as follows:
  - **No due date:** no ideal line, with a note saying why. A projected date is still shown.
  - **Due date changed:** the current due date is used.
  - **Overdue:** the chart runs to today.
  - **Closed milestone:** the chart ends at its close date.
  - **Item added after it was already closed:** the total rises but the open count doesn't.
  - **Empty milestone:** an empty-state message instead of a chart.
- [ ] AC8: Given a viewer who can't read the milestone's issues or pull requests, then neither the chart nor its data endpoint reveals them. A viewer who can read only one kind sees only that kind, and a reader of pull requests only sees pull requests by default.
- [ ] AC9: All new UI strings are in `options/locale/locale_en-US.json`.
- [ ] AC10: Unit tests cover the timeline replay (close/reopen, add, remove and move between milestones, add-after-closed), the ideal line and the projection. Integration tests cover the pull request toggle and the permission rules.

## Out of Scope
- An `/api/v1` endpoint for the burndown data.
- Story points or weights. Gitea has none, so every item counts as one.
- Burndown charts on the milestones list or on the user dashboard.
- A per-viewer time zone. Days follow the instance's time zone, the one due dates are stored in.
- History of issues later transferred to another repository: they drop out of every past day, because history is read for the milestone's own repository.

## Open Questions
None. Resolved during implementation:
- With no due date, the projected finish date is still shown, though the original spec said to hide it, because a finish date is useful without a deadline. Only the ideal line is hidden.
- A projection more than a year past the chart is stated in the summary but not drawn, so it can't squash the history.

## Design Decision
**Decision:** Rebuild each milestone's history when the chart is requested, by replaying its items' timeline comments (milestone changes, closes, merges and reopens), and serve it from a separate JSON endpoint that the page loads after it renders.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- A daily snapshot table filled by a scheduled job, which the chart reads directly.
- Deriving the chart from each issue's current `created_unix` and `closed_unix`, as the Activity tab's issues chart (#13) does.

**Rationale:** Snapshots need a migration and a new scheduled job, and they only start recording on the day they ship, so every existing milestone would have no history. Current timestamps can't show an issue that was reopened, or one that moved between milestones, which AC2 requires. Replaying comments works for every existing milestone straight away, needs no schema change, and is exact for anything Gitea recorded.

**Consequences:**
- The milestone columns on `comment` aren't indexed and `comment` has no `repo_id`. The query is bounded by the indexed comment type and a join on the repository's issues, and runs on its own lazy request so it can't slow the issue list.
- Issues migrated from other platforms have no milestone comments. The replay falls back to each issue's row and always ends on the database's current state, so the chart agrees with the progress bar.
- The milestone pages admit readers of issues *or* pull requests, so the endpoint filters by kind for each viewer (AC8).

### Further decisions made during implementation
- **Count issues by default, pull requests on request (AC6).** Alternative: always count both, as the progress bar does. The issue asked for a toggle defaulting to issues, and per-kind permission filtering makes either default safe.
- **The ideal line and the projection start at the first day with work (AC1, AC4),** not the creation day. Alternative: the creation day. Sprint milestones are usually created before they're filled, and counting from creation draws a flat ideal line at zero and reads the work arriving as work growing.
- **The projection uses the net burn rate over the last 14 days of work (AC4).** Alternative: the close rate alone. A net rate counts scope added mid-sprint, so it doesn't promise a date that new scope keeps pushing back.

## Scope
**Large** (`scope: large`), counted by the team as two mediums. The core is the timeline-replay engine, plus scope markers, projection, the pull request toggle, permission filtering, a data endpoint, the chart and its tests.

## Implementation notes
- Model: `models/issues/milestone_history.go` reads the history; service: `services/issue/milestone_burndown.go` (`CalcMilestoneBurndown` is pure and tested with a fixed clock and zone); route: `GET /{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}/burndown`.
- Frontend: `web_src/js/components/RepoMilestoneBurndown.vue`, following the Chart.js pattern of the Activity charts, with its logic in `RepoMilestoneBurndown.utils.ts`.
- Related to #13 (the Activity tab issues chart) but independent of it.

## Source
Personal use and our team's workflow: we plan work in fixed-length sprints with due dates, and a burndown chart is the standard way scrum teams track whether a sprint is on track. It's also a gap compared with Jira and GitLab, which offer milestone burndown charts.

Closes #14

## What changed

The milestone page (`/{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}`) now has a burndown chart above the issue list, folded under a "Burndown" heading that collapses. It shows:

- **Remaining:** open items at the end of each day, stepping on the day each change happened.
- **Total in milestone:** a dashed line with ▲ where items were added and ▼ where they were removed. The milestone's first day of work is its plan, so it is not marked.
- **Ideal:** a straight line from the first day with work down to zero on the due date.
- **Projected finish:** a dotted line extrapolated from the net burn rate over the last 14 days. A one-line summary says in words whether that is early, on the due date or late, or why there is no projection yet.
- **Hover details:** hovering a day lists the items that changed on it (closed, reopened, added, removed; a merge counts as closed). The same list appears under the chart with a link to each item, since links can't be clicked inside a canvas tooltip. It starts on the latest day with changes.
- **Include pull requests:** a checkbox, off by default, kept in the page URL as `include_pulls=1` without disturbing the issue list's own filters.

History is rebuilt from timeline comments (milestone changes, closes, merges and reopens), not from the current state. There is no schema change and no migration. The chart loads from its own endpoint, `GET /{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}/burndown`, so the issue list stays as fast as before.

## Why

A milestone page shows only a progress bar, so there is no way to tell whether a milestone is on track, when scope changed, or when it will finish. Acceptance criteria, in the order the issue lists them:

- **AC1** (chart with actual and ideal lines): the remaining and ideal lines. The axis runs from the first day to whichever is latest of today, the due date and the projection.
- **AC2** (history rebuilt from timeline events): each item's milestone, close, merge and reopen comments are replayed. Issues migrated in without those comments fall back to their row, and the replay always ends on the database's current state, so today's count matches the progress bar.
- **AC3** (scope additions and removals marked): ▲ and ▼ on the total line.
- **AC4** (projection shown only with enough data): hidden with under two days of history, when nothing has burned down over the window, when the work is done, or when the milestone is closed.
- **AC5** (hovering a day lists what changed): in the tooltip, and repeated with links under the chart.
- **AC6** (pull request toggle, off by default, in the URL): `include_pulls=1`; the checkbox reads it on load and writes it on change.
- **AC7** (edge cases): no due date hides the ideal line and says why; a changed due date uses the current one; an overdue milestone runs to today; a closed milestone ends on its close date (or on a later change, so the last point still matches the counters); an item added already closed widens the total but not the remaining count; an empty milestone shows a message instead of a chart.
- **AC8** (no access without permission, nothing private leaked): the endpoint sits in the same route group, with the same guards, as the milestone page. The milestone pages let in anyone who can read issues *or* pull requests, so the server counts and lists a kind only if the viewer can read it, and the checkbox is hidden from viewers who can't read pull requests.
- **AC9** (strings in `locale_en-US.json`): every visible string is under `repo.milestones.burndown.*`.
- **AC10** (unit tests for replay, toggle, ideal and projection): see below.

Deliberate differences from the issue's wording:
- The ideal line starts on the **first day with work**, not the creation day. Otherwise a milestone created empty and filled the next day draws a flat line at zero.
- A due date more than a year past the chart is not drawn. The test fixtures' year-9999 due date would otherwise flatten the chart.

## How it was tested

- **Go unit tests** (`models/issues/milestone_history_test.go`, `services/issue/milestone_burndown_test.go`):
  - The calculation is a pure function that takes `now` and a time zone, so 23 table cases cover every replay path: scope creep, items leaving, reopen, merge, an item added already closed, each fallback for missing history, the database winning when comments disagree, both closed-milestone endings, late, early and windowed projections, and the ideal line's limits.
  - Every case also asserts that the last point matches the items' current state.
  - Separate tests cover the per-day change lists, and dates across the New York daylight-saving changes.
  - The query tests check that only this milestone's and repository's history is read, that events come back in order, and that the batched lookups return every row.
- **Integration tests** (`tests/integration/milestone_burndown_test.go`):
  - `RealLifecycle` closes, reopens and moves issues through the real API and checks the history records Gitea actually wrote. The final counts alone can't show that, because the replay ends on the database's state either way.
  - `PullRequestsOnRequest` checks the toggle.
  - Two tests switch off the issues unit or the pull request unit and check that nothing of that kind is counted or listed. Both were confirmed to fail when the permission check is removed.
  - The rest check not-found and private-repository access.
- **Vitest** (`RepoMilestoneBurndown.utils.test.ts`): the summary sentence, ideal and projection lines, scope markers, axis range, tooltip lines, URL handling for the toggle (the issue list's filters survive it) and item links.
- **E2E** (`tests/e2e/milestone-burndown.test.ts`): the chart renders with its summary and accessible label; a closed issue appears in the change list with the right link; the toggle starts off, writes the URL, survives a reload and clears; the chart collapses and expands; an empty milestone shows its message.
- **Checked by hand,** because canvas drawing and multi-day history can't be produced through the API in real time: screenshots against a synthetic two-week history (markers, tooltip contents, step timing, the change list while moving the pointer to it), in light and dark themes, open and collapsed.

- `./.claude-students/check.sh`: ok (34 docs, guide 34/34).

- **R1 Projection counts the days before any work.** In `services/issue/milestone_burndown.go`, `CalcMilestoneBurndown` checks `last < burndownMinHistoryDays` and sets `window := min(burndownWindowDays, last)`. Both are measured from the milestone's creation, but the ideal line starts at `from`, the first day with work. If a milestone is created before its issues are added, the window reaches back to days where `Remaining == 0`, so the rate comes out negative.
- **R2 A closed milestone runs past its close date.** I agree with @vvchopra's R1 and reproduced it. A milestone closed on Jan 7 had an item that left it on Jan 6 and was closed on Jan 20. The chart produced 16 points ending **2026-01-20** instead of ending on Jan 7. Fix: skip zero-count deltas in `replayMilestoneItem`, and add the case as a test.
- **R3 Stale responses when the toggle changes during a fetch.** `fetchBurndown` in `RepoMilestoneBurndown.vue` doesn't drop superseded responses. If you tick the box and untick it again quickly, the chart can end up counting pull requests while the box is unchecked. Use a request counter or an `AbortController`. (This agrees with @vvchopra's R2 and CodeRabbit.)
- **R4 A reader of pull requests only sees an "empty" milestone.** In `MilestoneBurndownData`, when the issues unit is off or unreadable, both kinds are off by default. The chart then says "This milestone has no issues or pull requests yet." Default to pull requests in that case. (This agrees with @vvchopra's R3.)

### Issue #14: burndown chart on milestones (Large, counted as 2 mediums)
- **User story:** "As a team lead, I want a burndown chart for each milestone comparing actual progress against an ideal pace so that I can tell early whether we'll finish by the due date and see when scope changed."
- **Background:** the issue was first drafted for Carson in Sprint 0. You refined it into the course format. It was the product owner's request, and it took up your whole sprint. The report names it as one of the main reasons the sprint's scope changed.
- **What the chart shows:**
  - **Remaining:** open items at the end of each day.
  - **Total in milestone:** marked ▲ on days items were added and ▼ on days they were removed.
  - **Ideal:** a straight line from the first day with work down to zero on the due date.
  - **Projected finish:** a dotted line plus a one-line summary.
  - **Hover details:** hovering a day lists what changed. The same list appears under the chart with links, because links can't be clicked inside a canvas tooltip.
  - **"Include pull requests" checkbox:** off by default, and saved in the URL as `include_pulls=1`.
  - The chart can be collapsed.
- **10 acceptance criteria:**
  - AC1: actual and ideal lines
  - AC2: history rebuilt from timeline events
  - AC3: scope markers
  - AC4: projection only when there is enough history
  - AC5: hover details
  - AC6: pull request toggle
  - AC7: edge cases (no due date, changed due date, overdue, closed milestone, item added already closed, empty milestone)
  - AC8: permissions
  - AC9: every string in `locale_en-US.json`
  - AC10: tests

### Design decision (D3): know this one well
- **Decision:** rebuild each milestone's history when the chart is requested, by replaying timeline comments (milestone changes, closes, merges, reopens). The data comes from a separate JSON endpoint, `GET /{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}/burndown`, which the page loads after it renders.
- **Alternatives considered:**
  1. A daily snapshot table filled by a scheduled job.
  2. Building the chart from each issue's current `created_unix` and `closed_unix`, the way the Activity tab's chart (#13) does.
- **Why:**
  - Snapshots need a migration and a new scheduled job, and they only start recording on the day they ship, so existing milestones would have no history.
  - Current timestamps can't show an issue that was reopened or moved between milestones.
  - Replaying comments needs no schema change and works on old milestones straight away.
- **Consequences:**
  - The milestone columns on `comment` aren't indexed. The lazy endpoint keeps the issue list fast.
  - Migrated issues have no milestone comments, so the replay falls back to each issue's row. It always ends on the database's current state, so the last point matches the progress bar.
  - The endpoint has to filter by kind (issues or pull requests) for each viewer.
- **Further decisions made during implementation:**
  - Count issues by default and pull requests on request.
  - Start the ideal line and the projection at the first day with work, not the creation day, because sprint milestones are often created empty.
  - Base the projection on the net burn rate over the last 14 days, so scope added mid-sprint is counted.
  - With no due date, still show the projection and hide only the ideal line.
  - Don't draw a projection more than a year past the chart.

### Where the code lives
- **Model:** `models/issues/milestone_history.go`
- **Service:** `services/issue/milestone_burndown.go`. `CalcMilestoneBurndown` is a pure function that takes `now` and a time zone, so it's easy to test.
- **Route:** `routers/web/repo/milestone.go` (`MilestoneBurndownData`)
- **Frontend:** `web_src/js/components/RepoMilestoneBurndown.vue` (Chart.js), with its logic in `.utils.ts`

Multi-select dropdown ARIA state and announcements
> Sub-issue of #25 · **P3 — Sprint 2 carryover** · estimate **5 points** (medium) · blocked by nothing

## User Story
As a screen reader user labelling an issue, I want to hear which options are already selected and
hear confirmation when I add or remove one, so that I can tell what state the label list is in
without looking at it.

## User Scenario
A user opens the label menu on an issue. As they arrow through the options, each one is announced
with whether it is selected. They press Enter on "bug"; the reader announces that bug was added.
They arrow to it again, press Enter, and hear that bug was removed. At no point do they have to
guess by counting.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given a multiple-selection dropdown, then its popup carries `aria-multiselectable="true"`
      and every option carries `aria-selected` set to `true` or `false` — not merely the `active`
      class the current patch relies on.
- [ ] AC2: Given such a dropdown, when an option's selected state changes by keyboard or mouse,
      then its `aria-selected` updates in the same interaction.
- [ ] AC3: Given such a dropdown, when a selection is added or removed, then a polite live region
      announces which item and whether it was added or removed, using localised strings.
- [ ] AC4: Given a selection label with a delete icon, then the icon's accessible name includes
      that label's text rather than a bare "remove" — extending what `updateSelectionLabel` in
      `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.ts` does today.
- [ ] AC5: Given the issue label sidebar and the repository topics setting, when operated entirely
      by keyboard, then options can be selected and deselected and the resulting form submits the
      same values as before the change.
- [ ] AC6: `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/aria.md` no longer says multiple selection is unsupported;
      it describes what now works and what still does not.
- [ ] AC7: Unit tests in `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.test.ts` cover AC1, AC2 and AC4.

## Out of Scope
- Replacing these dropdowns with the component from #61. This issue improves the Fomantic patch
  in place; the two lines of work are deliberately independent.
- Single-selection dropdowns and menus.
- The VoiceOver "opened by mouse, arrow keys dead" bug in `aria.md`, which is a consequence of
  `aria-activedescendant` and is only fixed by migrating off Fomantic.

## Open Questions
- Whether one shared live region for the whole page is enough, or each dropdown needs its own.
  Proposed: one shared region created on demand, since two dropdowns are never operated at once.

## Design Decision
**Decision:** Extend the existing patch in `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.ts` rather than
replacing these dropdowns, and drive the announcements from the patched `onLabelCreate` and
selection callbacks that the module already delegates.

**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Wait for the #61 component to grow multi-select support and
migrate these dropdowns to it. (b) Observe the DOM with a `MutationObserver` on the selection
label container and announce from there.

**Rationale:** (a) leaves the label, assignee and reviewer selectors — the dropdowns a maintainer
touches most — unusable for the whole of Sprint 1 and probably Sprint 2, because multi-select is
the hardest variant to reimplement; an in-place fix delivers value now and is thrown away cleanly
later. (b) works without touching Fomantic's callbacks but cannot distinguish a label added by the
user from one rendered during initialisation, so the page would announce every pre-existing label
on load.

**Consequences:** Easier — ships within the sprint, touches one file plus its test, and is
independent of the #61/#62 line so two people can work in parallel without conflicts. Harder —
it adds code to a file that is explicitly meant to be deleted one day, so the work is temporary by
design; the note added to `aria.md` under AC6 should say so, and `dropdown.ts` grows further past
the size at which it is comfortable to review.

<!-- Paste-ready additions for issue #63. Paste the section below under the existing
"## Design Decision" in the issue body, and apply the AC edits listed at the end.
This file is a drafting aid; it is not meant to be committed. -->

### Design decisions by Vishav Chopra (@vvchopra)

These were made while starting implementation, after reading the code the original spec targets.
The original decision above (extend the Fomantic patch in place, independent of #61/#62) stands.

#### Decision 2: Cover the issue sidebar combo list as well as Fomantic multi-selects

**Decision:** Patch both multi-select mechanisms: Fomantic `multiple` dropdowns in
`web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.ts`, and the issue sidebar's multiple-mode combo lists
(labels, assignees, reviewers, projects) in `web_src/js/features/repo-issue-sidebar-combolist.ts`.

**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Fomantic multi-selects only, dropping the label sidebar from AC5
and filing it as a follow-up. (b) The sidebar combo list only, leaving AC4 for later.

**Rationale:** The issue label sidebar is not a Fomantic multiple-selection dropdown. It is a plain
`ui dropdown` whose selection is a `.checked` class toggled by `IssueSidebarComboList`, with no
selection labels and no `onLabelCreate` callback, so changing `dropdown.ts` alone cannot satisfy
the user story or AC5. Its items also sit inside a nested `.scrolling.menu`, which the existing
`updateMenuItem` pass never reaches, so today they get no `role` at all. Option (a) would leave the
scenario in this issue unfixed; option (b) would leave the topic and protected-branch pickers, and
the `data-value` bug under Decision 5, unfixed.

Closes #63

## What changed

Multi-select dropdowns now expose their selection state to assistive technology and announce
changes, and keyboard focus no longer drops to the page when an option is picked with Enter.

- **Shared announcer** (`web_src/js/modules/aria-announce.ts`). This is one polite `role="status"`
  live region, appended to `<body>` on first use, and it reads localised "Selected "%s"" /
  "Deselected "%s"" messages. Two strings were added to `locale_en-US.json` and `window.config.i18n`.
- **Fomantic multiple-selection dropdowns** (repo topics, branch/tag protection user and team
  pickers), in `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.ts`:
  - the listbox gets `aria-multiselectable="true"`, and every option gets `aria-selected`, which
    is refreshed after each add or remove;
  - additions and removals are announced, but selections present when the page loads are not;
  - each label's delete icon is named after the label's visible text, not its `data-value`. In
    the protected-branch pickers the value is a user or team ID, so screen readers used to hear
    *Remove item "12"*.
  - items in a nested `.scrolling.menu` now get their `role` and `id`.
- **Issue sidebar pickers** (labels, assignees, reviewers, projects), in
  `web_src/js/features/repo-issue-sidebar-combolist.ts`. These are not Fomantic multi-selects;
  their selection is a `.checked` class. They now keep `aria-selected` in step with that class and
  announce each toggle. That includes a scoped label replacing another, which announces both
  changes, and "Clear labels", which announces every removed item.
- **Focus fixes** (Decision 6). Both bugs also exist on `main`:
  - a `GITEA-PATCH` in `web_src/fomantic/build/components/dropdown.js` stops Fomantic's IE11
    workaround from blurring the dropdown itself when an item is picked. In the sidebar, that blur
    had closed the menu and saved after every Enter;
  - `initGlobalEnterQuickSubmit` (`web_src/js/features/common-form.ts`) now skips an Enter that a
    widget already handled. Before, adding a topic with Enter also clicked **Save** and closed the
    editor.
- **Docs.** `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/aria.md` now describes what works and what still does not.

## Why

Screen reader users labelling an issue could not tell which options were selected, got no
confirmation when they added or removed one, and lost focus after every pick. This PR satisfies:

- **AC1:** popups are multiselectable and every option carries `aria-selected`, for both
  Fomantic multiples and the sidebar pickers.
- **AC2:** `aria-selected` updates in the same interaction, by keyboard or mouse.
- **AC3:** a polite live region announces which item changed and how, using localised strings.
- **AC4:** delete icons are named by the label's visible text.
- **AC5:** the label sidebar and the topics editor can be operated entirely by keyboard, and they
  submit the same values as before.
- **AC6:** `aria.md` no longer says multiple selection is unsupported.
- **AC7:** unit tests cover AC1, AC2 and AC4. This was extended to the sidebar pickers per the
  spec edits.

## How it was tested

- **Unit tests (Vitest)**, one per acceptance criterion, all checking DOM state rather than
  implementation details:
  - `aria-announce.test.ts`: there is one region on `<body>`; messages in the same window are
    batched; the region is recreated after removal, and stale queued messages are dropped;
    strings are localised.
  - `fomantic/dropdown.test.ts`: AC1–AC4 against a real Fomantic multiple dropdown whose values
    are IDs; single-selection dropdowns stay untouched; nested scrolling-menu items get roles;
    picking an item keeps focus on the dropdown (this covers the `GITEA-PATCH`).
  - `repo-issue-sidebar-combolist.test.ts`: initial state without announcing, toggle, scoped
    replacement, clear-selection, the unchanged form value, and single mode not announcing.
  - `common-form.test.ts` (new): Enter in a bare `.ui.form` still clicks the primary button,
    but not when a widget already prevented the key.
- **E2E (Playwright)**, in `tests/e2e/multiselect-aria.test.ts`. This drives the real keyboard flows
  for AC5, which unit tests can't reach because they depend on Fomantic's keyboard handling and
  the global Enter handler working together:
  - labels: select, deselect and reselect by keyboard, checking focus and the announcement each
    time, then confirming the saved label;
  - topics: start from a seeded topic (which must not be announced), add one by keyboard, remove it
    with Backspace, save, and check the result.
- **By hand:** I followed the same flows with the browser and DevTools, including inspecting the
  delete-icon names in the protected-branch user picker. I used the live narrarator and the arrow keys to navigate and read the dropdown menus, as shown in the screenshot.
- **Root cause of the focus bugs:** I confirmed both by instrumenting `blur()`/`focus()` calls
  during a keyboard pick, and checked them against a build of `main`.

The concurrent Vitest config (`sequence.concurrent: true`) means the DOM-sharing groups run with
`{concurrent: false}`.

## Design

This follows the issue's Design Decision (extend the Fomantic patch in place), plus my Decisions
2–6 in the issue:

- Decision 2: cover both the Fomantic multi-selects and the sidebar pickers.
- Decision 3: one shared live region on `<body>`.
- Decision 4: the sidebar announces on each toggle.
- Decision 5: delete icons are named by visible text.
- Decision 6: fix the focus loss on Enter here.

The Decision 6 Fomantic patch also changes focus behaviour for every dropdown without a search
input: after a pick, focus stays on the dropdown instead of moving to `<body>`.

// Copyright 2026 The Gitea Authors. All rights reserved.
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT

package issue

import (
	"cmp"
	"context"
	"math"
	"slices"
	"time"

	issues_model "gitea.dev/models/issues"
	"gitea.dev/modules/setting"
	"gitea.dev/modules/timeutil"
)

// BurndownStatus says what the chart can tell about when a milestone will finish.
type BurndownStatus string

const (
	BurndownEmpty            BurndownStatus = "empty"             // nothing has ever been in the milestone
	BurndownDone             BurndownStatus = "done"              // every item in it is closed
	BurndownClosed           BurndownStatus = "closed"            // the milestone was closed with items still open
	BurndownProjected        BurndownStatus = "projected"         // a finish date could be extrapolated
	BurndownNotBurning       BurndownStatus = "not_burning"       // remaining work has not fallen over the window
	BurndownInsufficientData BurndownStatus = "insufficient_data" // too few days of history to extrapolate
)

const (
	burndownWindowDays     = 14  // the projection extrapolates the net burn rate over at most this many days
	burndownMinHistoryDays = 2   // a rate over fewer days is noise, not a trend
	burndownHorizonDays    = 365 // a due date further out than this past the chart is not drawn
)

// BurndownPoint is the state of a milestone at the end of one day.
type BurndownPoint struct {
	Date      string `json:"date"`      // "YYYY-MM-DD" in the instance zone, so every viewer sees the same day
	Remaining int    `json:"remaining"` // items in the milestone and open
	Scope     int    `json:"scope"`     // items in the milestone, open or closed
	Added     int    `json:"added"`     // items that joined the milestone this day, after its first day of work
	Removed   int    `json:"removed"`   // items that left the milestone this day, after its first day of work

	Changes []BurndownChange `json:"changes,omitempty"` // what moved the counts this day, in order; omitted on quiet days
}

// BurndownChangeKind is how one item changed the milestone's counts.
type BurndownChangeKind string

const (
	BurndownChangeClosed   BurndownChangeKind = "closed" // a merge counts as a close
	BurndownChangeReopened BurndownChangeKind = "reopened"
	BurndownChangeAdded    BurndownChangeKind = "added"
	BurndownChangeRemoved  BurndownChangeKind = "removed"
)

// BurndownChange is one item that changed the milestone's counts on a day.
type BurndownChange struct {
	Index  int64              `json:"index"`
	Title  string             `json:"title"`
	IsPull bool               `json:"isPull"`
	Kind   BurndownChangeKind `json:"kind"`
}

// BurndownOptions says which kinds of item to count. A caller must leave out any kind the viewer cannot read.
type BurndownOptions struct {
	Issues bool
	Pulls  bool
}

// BurndownIdeal is the straight line from the first day with work to zero on the due date.
type BurndownIdeal struct {
	From      string `json:"from"`
	FromValue int    `json:"fromValue"`
	To        string `json:"to"` // the due date; the line always ends at zero
}

// MilestoneBurndown is everything the milestone page charts.
type MilestoneBurndown struct {
	Points      []BurndownPoint `json:"points"`
	Deadline    string          `json:"deadline"` // empty when there is no due date, or it is too far out to draw
	Ideal       *BurndownIdeal  `json:"ideal"`
	Status      BurndownStatus  `json:"status"`
	Projected   string          `json:"projected"`   // set only when Status is projected
	DaysLate    *int            `json:"daysLate"`    // projected finish minus the due date; negative is early
	CompletedOn string          `json:"completedOn"` // set only when Status is done
}

type burndownState struct {
	inScope bool
	open    bool
}

type burndownDelta struct {
	at        int64
	remaining int
	scope     int
	item      *issues_model.MilestoneItem
}

func (d burndownDelta) moves() bool {
	return d.remaining != 0 || d.scope != 0
}

// kind names the change for the day's list; a change of scope outranks a close, since an item that
// joins already closed was added, not closed. It is empty when the counts did not move.
func (d burndownDelta) kind() BurndownChangeKind {
	switch {
	case d.scope > 0:
		return BurndownChangeAdded
	case d.scope < 0:
		return BurndownChangeRemoved
	case d.remaining < 0:
		return BurndownChangeClosed
	case d.remaining > 0:
		return BurndownChangeReopened
	}
	return ""
}

func (s burndownState) counts() (remaining, scope int) {
	if s.inScope {
		scope = 1
		if s.open {
			remaining = 1
		}
	}
	return remaining, scope
}

// diff is the change in the milestone's counts when an item moves from s to next
func (s burndownState) diff(next burndownState, at int64) burndownDelta {
	r0, s0 := s.counts()
	r1, s1 := next.counts()
	return burndownDelta{at: at, remaining: r1 - r0, scope: s1 - s0}
}

// replayMilestoneItem turns one item's comments into changes to the milestone's counts. Missing history
// is filled in so the replay always ends where the database is now: an item in the milestone with no
// comment saying it joined (migrated issues have none) joins when it was created or the milestone was,
// and a closed item with no close comment closes at its closed_unix.
func replayMilestoneItem(item issues_model.MilestoneItem, events []issues_model.MilestoneEvent, milestoneID, milestoneCreated int64) []burndownDelta {
	events = slices.Clone(events) // synthetic events are appended below
	created := int64(item.CreatedUnix)
	var firstScope *issues_model.MilestoneEvent
	hasClose := false
	for i := range events {
		switch events[i].Type {
		case issues_model.CommentTypeMilestone:
			if firstScope == nil {
				firstScope = &events[i]
			}
		case issues_model.CommentTypeClose, issues_model.CommentTypeMergePull:
			hasClose = true
		}
	}

	// synthetic events take id 0 so they sort before a real comment in the same second
	joinAt := max(created, milestoneCreated)
	if firstScope == nil && item.MilestoneID == milestoneID {
		events = append(events, issues_model.MilestoneEvent{Type: issues_model.CommentTypeMilestone, MilestoneID: milestoneID, CreatedUnix: timeutil.TimeStamp(joinAt)})
	} else if firstScope != nil && firstScope.MilestoneID != milestoneID {
		// its first recorded move is out of the milestone, so it was in it before then
		joinAt = min(joinAt, int64(firstScope.CreatedUnix))
		events = append(events, issues_model.MilestoneEvent{Type: issues_model.CommentTypeMilestone, MilestoneID: milestoneID, CreatedUnix: timeutil.TimeStamp(joinAt)})
	}
	if item.IsClosed && !hasClose {
		// a close time of zero predates the item, so clamp it as the Activity issues chart does
		closedAt := max(int64(item.ClosedUnix), created)
		events = append(events, issues_model.MilestoneEvent{Type: issues_model.CommentTypeClose, CreatedUnix: timeutil.TimeStamp(closedAt)})
	}
	slices.SortFunc(events, issues_model.CompareMilestoneEvents)

	state := burndownState{open: true}
	lastAt := created
	deltas := make([]burndownDelta, 0, len(events)+1)
	for _, e := range events {
		next := state
		switch e.Type {
		case issues_model.CommentTypeMilestone:
			if e.MilestoneID == milestoneID {
				next.inScope = true
			} else if e.OldMilestoneID == milestoneID {
				next.inScope = false
			}
		case issues_model.CommentTypeClose, issues_model.CommentTypeMergePull:
			next.open = false
		case issues_model.CommentTypeReopen:
			next.open = true
		}
		// a close or reopen while the item is outside the milestone moves no count; recording it would
		// stretch a closed milestone's chart to a change that never touched it
		if d := state.diff(next, int64(e.CreatedUnix)); d.moves() {
			deltas = append(deltas, d)
			lastAt = max(lastAt, d.at)
		}
		state = next
	}

	// the comments can still disagree with the row, for instance after a reopen whose close was never
	// recorded, and the row is the truth the progress bar shows, so end on it
	want := burndownState{inScope: item.MilestoneID == milestoneID, open: !item.IsClosed}
	if state != want {
		at := lastAt
		if state.open && !want.open {
			at = max(at, int64(item.ClosedUnix))
		}
		if d := state.diff(want, at); d.moves() {
			deltas = append(deltas, d)
		}
	}
	return deltas
}

// civilDay counts calendar days, so differences between dates ignore DST and zone offsets
func civilDay(t time.Time) int64 {
	return time.Date(t.Year(), t.Month(), t.Day(), 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC).Unix() / (24 * 60 * 60)
}

func startOfDay(unix int64, loc *time.Location) time.Time {
	t := time.Unix(unix, 0).In(loc)
	return time.Date(t.Year(), t.Month(), t.Day(), 0, 0, 0, 0, loc)
}

// CalcMilestoneBurndown charts a milestone from its items and their history. It reads no clock and no
// global zone, so it is tested with a fixed now and loc.
//
// Every item it is given counts, whatever its close reason; which kinds it is given is the caller's choice
// (see BurndownOptions).
func CalcMilestoneBurndown(m *issues_model.Milestone, items []issues_model.MilestoneItem, events []issues_model.MilestoneEvent, now time.Time, loc *time.Location) *MilestoneBurndown {
	result := &MilestoneBurndown{Points: []BurndownPoint{}, Status: BurndownEmpty}
	if len(items) == 0 {
		return result
	}

	byItem := make(map[int64][]issues_model.MilestoneEvent, len(items))
	for _, e := range events {
		byItem[e.IssueID] = append(byItem[e.IssueID], e)
	}
	var deltas []burndownDelta
	for i := range items {
		for _, d := range replayMilestoneItem(items[i], byItem[items[i].ID], m.ID, int64(m.CreatedUnix)) {
			d.item = &items[i]
			deltas = append(deltas, d)
		}
	}
	slices.SortStableFunc(deltas, func(a, b burndownDelta) int { return cmp.Compare(a.at, b.at) })

	start, end := int64(m.CreatedUnix), now.Unix()
	if start == 0 { // fixtures and some legacy rows have no creation time
		start = end
		if len(deltas) > 0 {
			start = deltas[0].at
		}
	}
	if m.IsClosed && m.ClosedDateUnix > 0 {
		// stop at the close, unless items moved after it: the last point must match today's counters
		end = int64(m.ClosedDateUnix)
		if len(deltas) > 0 {
			end = max(end, deltas[len(deltas)-1].at)
		}
		end = min(end, now.Unix())
	}
	end = max(end, start)

	firstDay, lastDay := startOfDay(start, loc), startOfDay(end, loc)
	remaining, scope, next := 0, 0, 0
	for day := firstDay; !day.After(lastDay); day = day.AddDate(0, 0, 1) {
		dayEnd := day.AddDate(0, 0, 1).Unix()
		point := BurndownPoint{Date: day.Format(time.DateOnly)}
		for ; next < len(deltas) && deltas[next].at < dayEnd; next++ {
			remaining += deltas[next].remaining
			scope += deltas[next].scope
			if deltas[next].scope > 0 {
				point.Added++
			} else if deltas[next].scope < 0 {
				point.Removed++
			}
			if kind := deltas[next].kind(); kind != "" {
				item := deltas[next].item
				point.Changes = append(point.Changes, BurndownChange{Index: item.Index, Title: item.Title, IsPull: item.IsPull, Kind: kind})
			}
		}
		point.Remaining, point.Scope = remaining, scope
		result.Points = append(result.Points, point)
	}
	points := result.Points
	last := len(points) - 1

	// what the milestone holds on its first day of work is its plan, not a change to it, so only
	// later days are marked; otherwise every chart would open on an "added" marker
	from := slices.IndexFunc(points, func(p BurndownPoint) bool { return p.Scope > 0 })
	for i := 0; i <= from; i++ {
		points[i].Added, points[i].Removed = 0, 0
		points[i].Changes = slices.DeleteFunc(points[i].Changes, func(c BurndownChange) bool {
			return c.Kind == BurndownChangeAdded || c.Kind == BurndownChangeRemoved
		})
		if len(points[i].Changes) == 0 {
			points[i].Changes = nil // keep quiet days out of the JSON
		}
	}

	var deadlineDay time.Time
	if m.DeadlineUnix > 0 {
		deadlineDay = startOfDay(int64(m.DeadlineUnix), loc)
		if civilDay(deadlineDay)-civilDay(lastDay) > burndownHorizonDays {
			deadlineDay = time.Time{} // the fixtures' year 9999, say: drawing it would flatten the chart
		} else {
			result.Deadline = deadlineDay.Format(time.DateOnly)
		}
	}

	if from >= 0 && !deadlineDay.IsZero() {
		fromDay := firstDay.AddDate(0, 0, from)
		if points[from].Remaining > 0 && deadlineDay.After(fromDay) {
			result.Ideal = &BurndownIdeal{From: points[from].Date, FromValue: points[from].Remaining, To: result.Deadline}
		}
	}

	switch {
	case points[last].Scope == 0:
		result.Status = BurndownEmpty
	case points[last].Remaining == 0:
		result.Status = BurndownDone
		done := last
		for done > 0 && points[done-1].Remaining == 0 && points[done-1].Scope > 0 {
			done--
		}
		result.CompletedOn = points[done].Date
	case m.IsClosed:
		result.Status = BurndownClosed
	// history counts from the first day with work: days before it hold nothing to burn, and a window
	// reaching back into them would read the work arriving as work growing
	case last-from < burndownMinHistoryDays:
		result.Status = BurndownInsufficientData
	default:
		window := min(burndownWindowDays, last-from)
		rate := float64(points[last-window].Remaining-points[last].Remaining) / float64(window)
		if rate <= 0 {
			result.Status = BurndownNotBurning
			break
		}
		projected := lastDay.AddDate(0, 0, int(math.Ceil(float64(points[last].Remaining)/rate)))
		result.Status = BurndownProjected
		result.Projected = projected.Format(time.DateOnly)
		if !deadlineDay.IsZero() {
			late := int(civilDay(projected) - civilDay(deadlineDay))
			result.DaysLate = &late
		}
	}
	return result
}

// GetMilestoneBurndown charts a milestone in the instance's zone, the zone its due date is stored in,
// counting only the kinds of item opts asks for.
func GetMilestoneBurndown(ctx context.Context, m *issues_model.Milestone, opts BurndownOptions) (*MilestoneBurndown, error) {
	scopeEvents, err := issues_model.GetMilestoneScopeEvents(ctx, m.RepoID, m.ID)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	movedIDs := make([]int64, 0, len(scopeEvents))
	for _, e := range scopeEvents {
		movedIDs = append(movedIDs, e.IssueID)
	}
	slices.Sort(movedIDs)
	items, err := issues_model.GetMilestoneItems(ctx, m.RepoID, m.ID, slices.Compact(movedIDs))
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	// a left-out kind is not counted and not listed, so a viewer never learns of items they cannot read
	items = slices.DeleteFunc(items, func(item issues_model.MilestoneItem) bool {
		return item.IsPull && !opts.Pulls || !item.IsPull && !opts.Issues
	})

	itemIDs := make([]int64, 0, len(items))
	for _, item := range items {
		itemIDs = append(itemIDs, item.ID)
	}
	stateEvents, err := issues_model.GetMilestoneStateEvents(ctx, itemIDs)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return CalcMilestoneBurndown(m, items, append(scopeEvents, stateEvents...), time.Now(), setting.DefaultUILocation), nil
}

These notes come from the code itself (`services/issue/milestone_burndown.go`, the route handler, the model queries and the Vue component), not only the PR description.

# Deep dive: issue #14 and PR #77, the milestone burndown chart

## The short pitch (memorise this)
> A Gitea milestone page only had a progress bar. I added a burndown chart that shows open items left each day against an ideal line to the due date. It marks the days scope was added or removed, and projects a finish date from the recent pace. The history is rebuilt from the issue timeline comments Gitea already stores, so it works for every existing milestone with no database migration.

## Timeline of the work
| When | What |
|---|---|
| Sprint 0 | Issue #14 was first drafted for Carson. You built #13, the Activity tab's issues chart (PR #41), which #77's chart follows the pattern of. |
| Oct 3 | Your AI session started (`2026-10-03_claude-code_issue-14-impl.md`). |
| Oct 6 | Core commits: history queries, then the calculation, then the JSON endpoint, then the chart, then e2e tests. Claude then found 3 acceptance criteria were missing (scope markers, hover details, the pull request toggle), and you added them plus the collapsible chart. |
| Oct 7 | Hover change list in the tooltip, merge from `main`. Ethan marked the spec **"Spec Reviewed: Not yet"** because it still needed the full course format. |
| Oct 8 | You refined the spec. You fixed the review findings in 4 commits. Ethan marked the spec **"Approved"**. Approved by Carson and Jack, merged Oct 8 at about 9 PM ET. |

## How it works, end to end

### 1. Request flow
1. You open `/{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}`. The page renders the issue list as before and passes `milestoneBurndownLink` to the frontend.
2. The Vue component (`RepoMilestoneBurndown.vue`) then fetches `GET /{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}/burndown[?include_pulls=1]`, served by `MilestoneBurndownData` in `routers/web/repo/milestone.go`.
3. Because the chart loads separately, a slow history query can never slow down the issue list.

### 2. Reading the history (`models/issues/milestone_history.go`)
- **`GetMilestoneScopeEvents(repoID, milestoneID)`:** milestone-change comments (`CommentTypeMilestone`) that moved an item into or out of this milestone. It joins on the repository's issues because `comment` has no `repo_id` column.
- **`GetMilestoneItems(...)`:** the milestone's current items plus every item that ever moved through it. That's how a removed item still shows on the days it was in the milestone.
- **`GetMilestoneStateEvents(itemIDs)`:** close, merge and reopen comments for those items, fetched in batches.
- **Ordering:** `CompareMilestoneEvents` sorts by time, then by comment ID, which is insertion order.

### 3. The replay (`replayMilestoneItem`, run once per item)
- **State:** each item has two flags, `inScope` (in this milestone or not) and `open`. Its contribution to the counts is `remaining = inScope && open` and `scope = inScope`.
- **Walking the comments:**
  - A milestone change sets `inScope`.
  - A close or merge sets `open = false`; a merge counts as a close.
  - A reopen sets `open = true`.
  - Each step yields a **delta**: the change to remaining and to scope.
- **Filling gaps with synthetic events:**
  - An item in the milestone with no "joined" comment, typically a migrated issue, joins at whichever is later of its own creation and the milestone's creation.
  - An item whose first recorded move is *out of* the milestone must have been in it before, so a join is added before that move.
  - A closed item with no close comment closes at its `closed_unix`.
- **Database wins:** if the comments still disagree with the issue's row, a final delta brings the item to the row's state. The last point therefore always matches the progress bar (AC2).
- **Fix from review:** a close or reopen while the item is *outside* the milestone moves no count, so it is dropped. Before the fix, those deltas stretched a closed milestone's chart past its close date.

### 4. Building the chart (`CalcMilestoneBurndown`)
- **It's a pure function.** It takes `now` and a time zone as arguments and reads no clock, so tests use a fixed date. The real caller passes `time.Now()` and `setting.DefaultUILocation`.
- **Range:** the chart runs from the milestone's creation day to today. A closed milestone ends at its close date, unless an item moved later, so the last point still matches today's counters.
- **Daily points:** it walks one day at a time, applying that day's deltas to get `Remaining`, `Scope`, `Added`, `Removed` and a `Changes` list.
- **First day with work** (`from`) is the first day with scope above zero. What the milestone holds that day is its plan, so ▲/▼ markers are suppressed up to that day.
- **Ideal line:** a straight line from `points[from].Remaining` down to 0 on the due date. It's only drawn if there's a due date, it falls after `from`, and there's work left. Due dates more than 365 days out are not drawn; the test fixtures' year-9999 date would flatten the chart.
- **Status:** one of `empty`, `done` (with `CompletedOn`), `closed`, `insufficient_data`, `not_burning` or `projected`.

### 5. The projection maths (expect a question on this)
1. If fewer than **2** days have passed since `from`, the status is `insufficient_data`.
2. Otherwise `window = min(14, last - from)`.
3. `rate = (Remaining[last - window] - Remaining[last]) / window`. This is the **net** burn rate: added scope cancels out closes.
4. If `rate <= 0`, the status is `not_burning`.
5. Otherwise `projected = today + ceil(Remaining / rate)` days, and `DaysLate = projected - due date`. A negative value means early.

Days are compared with `civilDay` (calendar-day arithmetic), so daylight-saving changes don't shift results. There are tests for the New York daylight-saving changes.

### 6. Permissions (AC8)
- **Route guard:** the endpoint sits in the same route group as the milestone page, behind `reqRepoIssuesOrPullsReader`. That lets in anyone who can read issues *or* pull requests.
- **Filtering by kind:**
  - `Issues = canReadIssues`
  - `Pulls = canReadPulls && (include_pulls || !canReadIssues)`
  - A kind the viewer can't read is removed **before** counting, so it's neither counted nor listed.
- **Pull-request-only readers** get pull requests by default. Before the fix, their chart always said the milestone was empty.
- **Tests:** two integration tests turn off the issues unit or the pull request unit and check that nothing of that kind leaks. Both were confirmed to fail when the check was removed.

### 7. Frontend (`RepoMilestoneBurndown.vue` and `.utils.ts`)
- **Chart:** built with Chart.js, like the Activity tab's charts.
- **Logic split out:** the summary sentence, ideal and projection lines, markers, axis and tooltips live in a plain `.utils.ts` file so Vitest can test them.
- **Toggle:** `include_pulls` is written into the URL with `history.replaceState`, keeping the issue list's own query parameters intact (AC6).
- **Race fix:** a `latestRequest` counter means only the latest response can update the chart. Without it, ticking and unticking quickly could leave pull requests counted while the box was unchecked.
- **Change list under the chart:** links can't be clicked inside a canvas tooltip, so the same list is shown below with real links.
- **Strings:** all visible text lives under `repo.milestones.burndown.*` in `locale_en-US.json`, with singular and plural day counts (AC9).

## Design decision (D3), in one breath
- **Chosen:** replay the timeline comments when the chart is requested, served from a separate endpoint.
- **Rejected:** daily snapshots (needs a migration and a scheduled job, and has no history for existing milestones), and current timestamps (can't show reopens or moves, so AC2 fails).
- **Costs:**
  - The query runs on columns that aren't indexed, which is mitigated by the lazy endpoint.
  - Migrated issues need the fallbacks.
  - Permissions have to be filtered by kind.
  - Issues transferred to another repo drop out of history.

**Other decisions:** issues by default; the ideal line starts at the first day with work; the projection uses the net rate over 14 days; with no due date, the projection still shows and only the ideal line is hidden.

## Testing (D4: the "test strategy with explanation" points)
- **Go unit tests:**
  - **23 table cases**, each asserting that the last point matches the database.
  - Paths covered: scope creep, items leaving, reopen, merge, item added already closed, each fallback, the database winning a disagreement, both closed-milestone endings, early, late and windowed projections, and the ideal line's limits.
  - Daylight-saving tests.
  - Query tests for scoping, ordering and batching.
- **Integration tests:**
  - `RealLifecycle` drives real API closes, reopens and moves. This proves Gitea writes the comments the replay expects; final counts alone couldn't show that, because the replay ends on the database either way.
  - `PullRequestsOnRequest` checks the toggle.
  - The 2 permission tests.
  - Not-found and private-repository access.
- **Vitest:** the chart logic in `.utils.ts`.
- **Playwright e2e:** the chart renders, the change-list link works, the toggle writes the URL and survives a reload, collapse works, an empty milestone shows its message, and (added after review) a stale response is dropped after a quick toggle.
- **By hand:** canvas drawing and multi-day history can't be produced through the API in real time. You checked them with screenshots of a synthetic two-week history in light and dark themes.

- `5fa694b26e`: default to pull requests for readers of pull requests only.

## Honest weaknesses (have an answer ready)
1. **The spec came after the code.** It was refined only on Oct 7–8 and approved on the last day. The team's Sprint 2 rule is now "don't branch until the spec is Approved."
2. **#77 was merged with `test-pgsql-shard-2` failing.**
   - **Cause:** events in the same second come back in a different order on PostgreSQL. It passes on SQLite, MySQL and MSSQL.
   - **Status:** listed as the first Sprint 2 task. I don't see a fix on `main` yet.
3. **The PR was huge:** about 23.5k lines added, mostly the AI log committed inside it, which made review harder.
4. **Late and large:** it took you the whole sprint and was opened on the last day, and the report names it as the main cause of the sprint's scope change.
5. **Leaning on AI.** Claude wrote most of the code and caught the 3 missing acceptance criteria. Your part: you chose the scope and design, reviewed and approved every commit, merged `main`, pushed, and fixed the review findings.

## Quick-fire Q&A
- **Why a separate endpoint?** So the possibly slow history query can't slow the issue list. The chart loads after the page renders.
- **Why no migration?** Gitea already records milestone, close, merge and reopen comments, so replaying them reconstructs history.
- **How do you know the chart is right today?** The replay always ends on the database row, and every test asserts that the last point matches the progress bar.
- **What's "net burn rate"?** Change in remaining over the window. Added scope counts against progress, so the projection doesn't over-promise.
- **Why start the ideal line at the first day with work?** Sprint milestones are often created empty. Starting at creation would draw the ideal line flat at zero and make the arriving work look like scope creep.
- **What counts as one unit?** Every issue or pull request counts as 1. Gitea has no story points, and points are out of scope.
- **What time zone?** The instance's (`setting.DefaultUILocation`), the one due dates are stored in, so every viewer sees the same days.
- **What's out of scope?** An `/api/v1` endpoint, story points, charts on the milestones list or dashboard, per-viewer time zones, and history for transferred issues.
